FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau the Cosmetics Sectional Committee, had been Products Division Council. of Indian approved Standards, after the by the Petroleum, draft Coal finalized by and Related

Cetyl alcohol is a white unctuous mixture of solid alcohols consisting chiefly of n-hexadecanol. is soluble in ethanol, ether, chloroform and toluene and insoluble in water. It conforms to formula: CHs ( CH2 ) lKH,OH

It the

Cetyl alcohol is an important ingredient in cosmetic products like creams, lotions, etc. either as such or after ethoxylation. It is obtained by high pressure hydrogenation of palmitic acid. In certain cosmetic products, a mixture of cetyl alcohol and stearyl alcohol gives better properties than pure cetyl alcohol. Cetearyl alcohol, a mixture of cetyl and stearyl alcohols. is an odourless, white, waxy solid which is It is slightly soluble in petroleum ether, ethanol soluble in diethyl ether, benzene and chloroform. and acetone and is insoluble in water. This standard provides specifications for pure cetyl alcohol, whereas requirement alcohol ( mixture of cetyl and stearyl alcohols ) are given for information only. This standard is essentially based on Cosmetic, Toiletries Specification For Cetyl alcohol and Cetearyl alcohol. Fragrance Association for cetearyl

( CTFA

)

For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test, shall be rounded off in accordance of significant with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values (.revised )`. The number places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

A-3.0 Acid value is the number of milligranls of potassium hydroxide required to neutralize free fatty acids in 1 g of sample. A-3.1 Reagents A-3.1.1 A-3.1.2 A-3.1.3 A-3.2 Alcoholic Sodium Hydroxide Methanol Isopropanol Procedure 0.1 N.

M = mass in g of the sample. A-5 A-5.1 DETERMINATION OF MOISTURE

Outline of the Method

The method determines the actual water content of the material by titration with Karl Fischer reagent which reacts quantitatively with water. A-5.2 Procedure

Weigh accurately about 10 g of the sample into a conical flask. Add about 25 ml of a 2 : 1 mixture of methanol : Isopropanol previously neutral&d with 0.1 N sodium hydroxide to a faint pink phenolphthalein colour. Warm to dissolve the sample. Titrate against 0.1 sodium hydroxide to the same faint pink colour. A-3.3 Calculation Acid value where T N= M= = ml of sodium hydroxide required for neutralization, normality of hydroxide solution, and mass in g of the sample. 3 T x N x 56.1 =pp M

Take about 20 g of material, weigh accurately and dctemline the moisture content by the procedure given in IS 2362 : 1973. A-6 DETERMINATION OF HYDROCARBON

The analysis measures the hydrocarbon content in fatty alcohols. The principle in the. analysis is the absorption of the fatty alcohols on silica gel, while the hydrocarbons are not absorbed. A-6.1 A-6.1.1 A-6.2 Reagents Pentane Procedure

Weigh accurately about 2 g of sample into a 100ml flask and add 50 ml of pentane to it. If it is an

IS 14137 : 1994 alcohol with a high melting point then it has to be melted first in a steam bath and weighed promptly and, after adding pentane, the mixture has to be heated. Take a glass tube of 50 cm length and 1.2 cm internal diameter. Fill the bottom of the tube with some spu11 glass and press it together with a metal rod. Fill up with powdered silica gel (800-200 mesh) and gently tap the tube against a wooden plate about 30 times until the column is 45 cm full. Place a loo-ml flask underneath the tube. Transfer the sample solution by a small funnel to a round flask with a long and narrow neck. Put the long necked flask upside down into the silica gel tube and allow the pentane to drip. When the round flask is empty, the sample flask is washed by SO-ml pentane, which is transferred to the long necked flask and dripped through the silica gel tube. This takes about two hours. After this, remove the lOO-ml flask in which the pentane, with extracts, is collected and put another 50 ml pentane through the silica gel collect it in a separate flask. For C,, and other aicohols with a high melting point, silica gel tube shall be heated with a heating bulb. The heating bulb is placed at a distance from the column sufficient to keep the alcohol in a liquid state. Care should be taken that the pentane does not boil. After the extraction is complete, evaporate the pentane from the loo-ml flask on the steam bath until about 5 ml solution is left in the flask. Transfer this solution to a dry and weighed (iI4) aluminium bowl. Wash the flask twice with 5 ml of pentane. Keep the aluminum bowl on the steam bath and gently evaporate the pentane. Watch the pentane evaporation closely, and when bubbling ceases, remove the bowl immediately. Keep the bowl in the vacuum desiccator at ambient temperature for 15 minutes. Weigh the aluminium bowl again (N). The difference in mass (N - M) gives the hydrocarbon weight. The second extraction with 50 ml pentanc is done in the same way and the hydrocarbon determination should not be more than 1 mg. A-6.3 Calculution Mass of hydrocarbon = Mass of sample = (N - M) x 100 where (1 N = mass in g of the residue, M = mass in g of the aluminium and (I = mass in g of the sample. A-7 GAS CHROMATOGRAI'HIC OF ACETYI, ALCOHOL FOR INDUSTRY A-7.0 General conditions given here are for 4 bowl, A-7.3 Injection port temperature Detector TYPC Temperature Calculation F.T.D. 300�C x 100 guidance only. The percentage of various fatty alcohols in a given sample is determined by gas chromatography. A-7.1 Outline of the Method

A sample of the material is dissolved in a suitable solvent (for example, hexane, cyclohexane, chloroform and petroleum ether) and is injected into the gas chromatograph where it is carried by the carrier gas from one end of the column to the other. During its movement, the constituents of the sample undergo distribution at different rates and ultimately get separated from one another. The separated constituents emerge from the end of the column one after another and are detected by suitable means whose response is related to the amount of a specific component leaving the column. A-7.2 Apparatus

A-7.2.1 Any suitable gas chromatograph and column capable of being operated under conditions suitable for resolving the individual constituents into distinct peaks may be used. The typical chromatogram for cetyl alcohol with the following chromatographic conditions is shown in Fig. 1. Sample size 0.1 to 0.2 microlitres as 50 percent solution in chloroform

A-7.3.1 Calculate from the peak areas ot' individual constituents shown on the chromatogram of the material, concentrations of constituents on the basis of peaks area on chromatogram obtained with known amount of pure constituents using the same apparatus under identical conditions.

IS 14137 : 1994 A-7.3.2

Area Measuremmt

(See Note)

Since normal peaks approximate a triangle, the area is measured by multiplying the peak height times the width of half height. The normal peak base is not taken since large deviations may be observed due to tailing or adsorption. The technique is rapid, simple and fairly accurate when peaks are symmetrical and of reasonable width. A-7.3.3

A-10.3.1 Place 2 g of sample accurately weighed in a plaGnum dish and incinerate for about 2 hours at 525 to 550 "C. Cool and add 1 to 2 ml of hydrochloric acid and 0.5 ml nitric acid and evaporate to dryness on the steam bath. Dissolve the residue in 5 ml hot water, evaporate to dryness and treat it with hydrofluoric acid. Evaporate again to dryness. Dilute it with water (about 50 ml). Filter the solulion, if necessary, with suction through a fine frilled glass filter and dilute the filtrate and washing to 100 ml in a graduated Flask. This solution shall be used for tests given in A-10.3.2 and A-11.2.
